meta.title: The G Form: Played in Pieces
meta.summary: The G form is the widest of the five and the hardest to hold whole, so it lives as three small triads instead, each one good for something specific.

spans.text: The G form of
C
sits with its barre at fret
, drawing a window across frets
. Every string in that window carries a chord tone — degrees
, low E to high e. Three of those dots are the roots you already know:
, and
. What is new here is everything sitting between them — the fifths and thirds that turn three roots into a full triad on every string.
This is the form you never end up holding whole, and the reason is exact rather than a general complaint about barre chords. The barre at fret
reaches strings 4, 3 and 2 only. String 5 sits at fret
, and strings 6 and 1 sit at fret

— a four-fret span, with your little finger asked to cover two strings that aren't even next to each other. It's the widest stretch of the five forms, and it is the one shape teachers and players agree on: the G form doesn't get held whole.

props.caption: Seven chord tones in the window. The barre only reaches the middle three strings — the rest gets played in pieces.

spans.text: So it gets played in pieces instead, and each piece earns its place separately — three small chords living inside one window.
The bottom three —
— is a full triad that walks back down the frets as it climbs the strings:
, then
, then
. It's a compact shape for the bottom of a progression — three low strings, one hand position, nothing above it needed.
The middle three sit at a single fret —
— one finger laid across three strings, and a complete triad falls out of it. This is the
most useful three notes
in the entire form: minimal effort, full chord.
The top three are the sharpest of the bunch:
. Read the degrees —

— and notice what's missing. There is no fifth here at all, and the chord is still unmistakably major, because the third is still in it. Of everything this chapter has to say about fragments, this is the clearest proof: the third is the note a fragment keeps, even when it has to let the fifth go.
There is a reason the top piece has to go without. Read the whole grip —
— and count: three roots, two thirds, and exactly
one
fifth, down at
. Take any piece of this form that doesn't include string 4 and you have left the only fifth behind. The window does hold a second one —
, on string 2 at fret 8 — but it isn't in the grip, so no piece you play reaches it.
A
and a
are enough to say major. The G form's top three strings are the proof — the
is the note you can afford to lose.

Put a root on the bottom string, a chord tone on every string in between, and a root on the top string, and you get a window that shows the chord's whole range at a glance — low to high, in one five-fret span. That's exactly why the G form is worth
seeing
even though it isn't worth holding: nowhere else on the neck can you look at one window and see this chord's entire reach.
